name: Choctaw-Chickasaw Banaha Bread
region: Choctaw and Chickasaw communities / Indigenous Americas
imageAlt: A bowl of dried corn kernels illustrating corn, the defining ingredient of Choctaw-Chickasaw banaha; this is not a photograph of the finished bread
imageCredit: Photo: Daderot, Wikimedia Commons, CC0. Ingredient image; not a photograph of finished banaha.
summary: Choctaw-Chickasaw banaha from the Chickasaw Nation's public recipe: a firm cornmeal dough wrapped in softened corn husks and boiled until set, with cooked beans as a documented variation.
lead: Cornmeal, hot water, salt and soda become a compact boiled bread when the dough is wrapped tightly in corn husks and cooked directly in simmering water.
about: The Chickasaw Nation publishes this dish specifically as Choctaw-Chickasaw Banaha Bread. Its formula is notably spare: cornmeal, hot water, baking soda and salt are formed into oblong portions, wrapped in softened corn shucks and boiled. The Nation also documents a version with cooked black-eyed peas or red beans. This page stays close to that public community recipe instead of treating banaha as a generic tamale or inventing additional seasonings.
story: Banaha belongs to living Choctaw and Chickasaw foodways centered on corn. The Chickasaw Nation preserves the recipe in its cultural foods collection, while Smithsonian programming has described banaha as a traditional Choctaw cornmeal dish and used it to introduce visitors to Choctaw food culture. The wrapper is functional as well as traditional: softened husks hold the stiff cornmeal mixture together while it cooks in water. Leftover banaha can be sliced and fried, a serving method the Chickasaw Nation also records.
caveat: This is a home rendering of a recipe the Chickasaw Nation has made public. Keep the Choctaw-Chickasaw attribution attached to the dish. The bean variation below is documented by the Nation, but it is optional rather than a required defining ingredient.
prepNotes: Simmer or soak dried corn husks in very hot water about 10 minutes so they bend without cracking; keep them submerged with a plate if necessary.
Add the hot water gradually. The mixture should hold an oblong shape in your hand rather than slump like cornbread batter.
Use two overlapping husks for small or torn wrappers and tie the center with a thin strip of husk or kitchen-safe cotton twine so water cannot wash the dough apart.
ingredients: 6 to 12 dried corn husks, softened in hot water
1/2 cup cooked black-eyed peas or red beans, drained well, optional documented variation
steps: Bring a deep pot of water to a boil. In a separate heatproof bowl cover the dried corn husks with very hot water for about 10 minutes, until supple enough to fold without splitting; drain and pat them lightly dry.

Whisk cornmeal, baking soda and salt together. Stir in about 1 1/4 cups of the hot water, then add the remaining water a little at a time until a stiff, evenly hydrated dough forms. If using the documented bean variation, fold in the drained cooked beans now.

Checkpoint: squeeze a handful. It should compact cleanly and hold its shape with no dry cornmeal pockets, but it should not ooze or spread. If crumbly, add hot water 1 tablespoon at a time; if loose, let it stand 3 minutes so the cornmeal can absorb moisture.

Divide into 6 portions and shape each into a small oblong roughly the size of a tennis ball. Place each portion on a softened husk, fold the long sides over the dough, fold the ends inward and tie the packet around the middle. Double-wrap any packet whose husk has holes or tears.
Lower the packets into the boiling water, cover the pot and adjust the heat to maintain a steady but not violent boil. Cook 40 minutes, keeping the packets submerged as much as practical.

Lift out one packet with tongs and rest it 3 minutes before opening carefully; trapped steam will be hot. The cornmeal should be fully set from edge to center, moist but not pasty, and the packet should smell distinctly of cooked corn rather than raw meal.

Drain the remaining banaha and serve warm. For leftovers, cool promptly, refrigerate, then slice about 1/2 inch thick and pan-fry until the cut faces are crisp and hot through, following the serving option documented by the Chickasaw Nation.
sources: Chickasaw Nation - Foods and cultural continuity

name: Somali Laxoox (Canjeero)
imageAlt: Somali laxoox, a soft fermented griddle flatbread with a porous, eye-covered surface
imageCredit: Photo: Gilabrand, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
summary: Somali laxoox, called canjeero in southern regions, made as an overnight-fermented wheat-and-sorghum batter and cooked on one side until the surface fills with characteristic holes or 'eyes.'
lead: A mildly sour batter cooks only from below and by trapped steam, creating a browned underside and the soft, porous top that Somali cooks recognize by its many eyes.
about: A 2022 in-field study of 46 Somali women documents the flatbread as laxoox in northern regions and canjeero in southern Somalia. Nearly all respondents used wheat flour, while many combined wheat with sorghum, maize, barley or other grains. Fermentation, a medium-hot griddle, one-sided cooking and a hole-filled surface are central characteristics. This practical home formula uses wheat plus sorghum and a very small amount of commercial yeast to make the process reproducible; the research makes clear that household fermentation systems and grain blends are far more varied.
story: The Journal of Ethnic Foods survey traces laxoox/canjeero through Somali household knowledge rather than a single standardized recipe. Historically sorghum and maize were important, while refined wheat became increasingly common. Fermented batter is commonly held overnight, and the bread is overwhelmingly associated with breakfast. Respondents paired it with sweet Somali tea, oil and sugar, suqaar, stews, liver, eggs, ghee and other foods. The study also distinguishes heritage cajiin methods and reserved fermented starter, or dhanaanis, from newer and diaspora adaptations.
caveat: Commercial yeast is a practical home-kitchen aid, not the default traditional ferment: the field study found respondents generally relied on wild fermentation or reserved fermented batter and did not regularly use commercial yeast. If you maintain an active laxoox/canjeero starter from a trusted household method, use that instead and adjust fermentation time by smell, bubbles and experience.
prepNotes: Ferment by signs, not only the clock
The batter is ready when bubbles are visible across the surface and it smells pleasantly fermented and lightly sour. A cool kitchen may require longer than 10 hours.
After fermentation it should flow from a ladle in a thick ribbon and spread with a circular motion, not sit like pancake dough.
A fitting lid traps steam so the top cooks without flipping; the many open holes and a dry, set surface are the visual checkpoint.
ingredients: 1/2 tsp instant yeast, practical home adaptation
2 1/4 cups room-temperature water, plus more after fermentation as needed
Neutral oil, for a very light film on the griddle
Sesame or other vegetable oil and sugar, optional for a documented breakfast serving style
Sweet Somali tea, eggs, suqaar or stew, optional accompaniments
steps: Whisk the all-purpose flour, sorghum flour, yeast and salt in a large bowl. Add 2 1/4 cups water and whisk vigorously for 2 minutes, scraping the sides, until no dry pockets remain and the batter is smooth enough to pour.
Cover loosely and leave at room temperature overnight, about 8 to 12 hours. Do not seal the container airtight.

Checkpoint before cooking: the surface should show obvious bubbles and the batter should smell mildly sour and fermented, not putrid or sharply unpleasant. If it shows no activity in a cool room, give it more time in a warmer location rather than increasing heat aggressively.
Whisk the fermented batter for 30 seconds. Add water 1 tablespoon at a time until it pours in a thick continuous ribbon; it should be thinner than American pancake batter but not watery.

Warm a flat cast-iron or nonstick griddle over medium heat. Wipe it with the thinnest film of oil. Pour about 1/3 cup batter near the center and use the ladle bottom to guide it outward in a spiral into a thin 7- to 8-inch round.
Cover immediately and cook 2 to 4 minutes without flipping. Keep the heat medium: the bread should steam and develop holes steadily rather than scorch before the top sets.

Checkpoint: the upper surface should be matte, soft and pockmarked with many open 'eyes,' with no wet batter remaining; the underside should be lightly to moderately browned and briefly crisp at first, while the interior stays soft and chewy.

Slide onto a plate and repeat, adjusting the heat if the bottoms darken before the tops cook. Serve warm for breakfast with sweet Somali tea and, according to preference, oil with sugar or savory accompaniments such as eggs, suqaar or stew.

name: Sri Lankan Kottu Roti
imageAlt: A plated serving of Sri Lankan kottu roti, chopped flatbread stir-fried with vegetables and seasonings
imageCredit: Photo: Janice99999999999, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
summary: Sri Lankan kottu roti with chopped godamba-style flatbread, cabbage, carrot, onion, curry leaves, chile and egg worked together over a very hot griddle until the roti absorbs the aromatic seasoning.
lead: Kottu is recognized as much by sound as appearance: chopped flatbread, vegetables and egg are rapidly mixed and cut together on a hot metal surface until the roti is chewy, browned at the edges and saturated with spice.
about: Kottu, also spelled koththu or kothu roti, is Sri Lankan chopped-flatbread street food. The defining technique is to chop and mix roti on a hot griddle with vegetables, aromatics, egg and often curry or meat. SBS documents both vegetarian and protein-rich forms and notes that two wide spatulas can substitute for the street vendor's paired metal paddles. Godamba roti is the characteristic bread; good frozen godamba or plain paratha is a practical substitute when that specific flatbread is unavailable.
story: Sri Lankan accounts closely associate kottu with evening street-food culture and the percussive clatter of metal blades on a griddle. The Tamil word koththu refers to chopping, which describes the action at the center of the dish. Modern kottu appears in many forms - vegetable, egg, chicken, seafood and cheese among them - so this page does not claim one topping combination is definitive. Instead it focuses on the shared technique: high heat, chopped roti, crisp-tender vegetables and enough seasoned moisture to flavor the bread without turning it soggy.
caveat: Plain paratha is a practical substitute documented in published home recipes, but it is not identical to Sri Lankan godamba roti. Keep the griddle hot and add only enough liquid to season the bread; a wet, stewed mixture loses the characteristic chewy-toasted texture.
prepNotes: Cut everything before heating the pan
Kottu moves quickly. Have the roti, vegetables, beaten eggs and seasonings beside the stove before you begin.
A large cast-iron griddle, plancha or widest heavy skillet gives moisture room to evaporate instead of steaming the vegetables.
Two spatulas recreate the motion safely
Use two wide metal spatulas to chop, scrape and toss. Keep both tools flat against the cooking surface and away from your fingers rather than imitating showy street-vendor blade work.
ingredients: 5 godamba roti or plain paratha, cooked, cooled and cut into 1/2-inch strips
1 medium carrot, cut into fine matchsticks
2 tsp Sri Lankan roasted curry powder
1/3 cup thin chicken or vegetable curry gravy, or low-sodium stock, added only as needed
1 tbsp soy sauce, optional modern home seasoning
1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
Lime or lemon wedges and chopped cilantro, for serving
steps: Heat a large flat griddle or heavy skillet over medium-high to high heat until a drop of water skitters and evaporates quickly. Add the oil, onion, garlic, ginger, curry leaves and chile; stir-fry 60 to 90 seconds until loudly sizzling and aromatic but not scorched.
Add carrot and cabbage and cook 2 to 3 minutes, tossing constantly. The vegetables should brighten and soften at their thin edges while retaining some crispness.
Add tomato, curry powder, cumin and black pepper. Cook 1 to 2 minutes, scraping the surface, until the tomato begins to collapse and the spice aroma becomes toasted rather than raw.
Push the vegetables to one side. Pour the eggs onto the bare hot surface and scramble until they form soft curds with no liquid egg remaining, then fold them through the vegetables.
Add the chopped roti. Using two broad spatulas, repeatedly chop down, scrape inward and toss for 3 to 4 minutes so the bread breaks into irregular bite-size pieces and picks up the seasoned oil.

Drizzle in about half the gravy or stock and the soy sauce if using. Continue chopping and tossing over high heat. Add the remaining liquid only if the bread still tastes dry; the pan should keep sizzling rather than bubbling like a stew.

Checkpoint: vegetables should be crisp-tender, egg fully set, and roti hot through with chewy centers, some browned edges and an even coating of spice. There should be no pool of liquid on the griddle and the aroma should be curry-leaf fragrant and lightly toasted.

Taste for salt, scrape up any browned flavorful bits and serve immediately with lime or lemon and cilantro. Kottu is best straight from the griddle while the contrast between soft-chewy bread and lightly crisp edges is strongest.
